description: Beginner-friendly team building a browser-based Space Mission Design Game where players plan and launch missions using real NASA facts. I handle web dev (HTML, CSS, JS) and game logic, my teammate handles research and the pitch. We’re learning as we go and keep it chill. Looking for: a UI/graphic designer, someone who likes writing or space facts, or anyone who can do sound and animation.
summary: Margins is a browser game where students design a complete robotic space mission. You pick a goal, build the spacecraft (rocket, power, antenna, computer, instruments), launch it, and see whether it survives. Mass, power, budget, data, communications and time all push against each other, so every upgrade has a cost. After each mission, the game explains in plain English why it worked or failed and what change would have fixed it.
details:
WHAT IT DOES

Margins turns mission design into something you can feel. Students rarely get to experiment with a whole mission, so the trade-offs stay abstract. In Margins you choose a mission (like mapping water ice at the Moon's south pole), build your spacecraft on screen, and watch six gauges react as you add parts: mass, power, budget, data, communications and time. A better instrument finds more science, but it is heavier, draws more power, produces more data and costs more.

HOW IT WORKS

1. Pick a destination and read the mission goal and requirements.

2. Build the spacecraft: bus, power system, antenna, onboard computer, attitude control, instruments, launch vehicle and orbit. Parts snap onto a spacecraft that visibly changes.

3. Run the Go/No-Go checklist, which checks mass, power, data, budget, time and launch vehicle compatibility.

4. Launch. Hazards such as solar flares happen during flight and you make decisions.

5. The debrief shows your score, stars, and a plain-English explanation of why the mission succeeded or failed, plus what change would have saved it. Then rerun with changes.

There is no single perfect design. Different combinations of spacecraft, instruments and orbits can reach the same goal, so players replay to improve science, cost and safety margins.

BENEFITS

Players learn why engineers keep margins, why more capable instruments cost more power and data, and why a mission to Mars needs a different power system than a mission to the Moon. Feedback explains reasons, not just pass or fail.

BUILT WITH

React, TypeScript, Vite, Vitest, SVG and Canvas graphics, Web Audio for sound, hosted on Netlify. The game rules are a separate, tested engine, so results are repeatable and explainable.
